card: Russian word order is free in grammar but not in meaning: what's known comes first, what's new comes last. **Ма́ма пришла́** (Mum has arrived) answers *what did Mum do?*; **Пришла́ ма́ма** (It's Mum!) answers *who came?* The end of the sentence carries the news.

sections.body: Endings already show who does what, so Russian uses order for the flow of information. A wrong order isn't ungrammatical, but it answers a different question.

sections.title: Known first, new last
sections.body: Answering *where's the book?*: **Кни́га на столе́.** Answering *what's on the table?*: **На столе́ кни́га.** Russian has no articles, and order does part of their job: **В ко́мнату вошла́ же́нщина** is *a woman came in*; **Же́нщина вошла́ в ко́мнату** is *the woman came in*.

sections.title: Neutral orders
sections.body: In a neutral statement: subject, verb, object (**Ма́ша чита́ет кни́гу**); time and place first (**Вчера́ в Москве́ шёл дождь**); an adjective before its noun; pronouns before the verb. **Я тебя́ люблю́** is the warm, ordinary order; **Я люблю́ тебя́** puts the weight on *you*.

mistakes.why: A new person in the scene goes last, after what's known (the room).

mistakes.wrong: Где моя́ кни́га? — Лежи́т кни́га на столе́.
mistakes.right: Где моя́ кни́га? — Она́ на столе́.
mistakes.why: The answer (where) is the news, so it goes at the end.

examples.en: There's a book on the table.
The book is on the table.
It was my brother who wrote this book.
